text:
Friday, 13 November 2026, attracted considerable attention because of an old prediction associated with the end of the world. According to a widely circulated claim, today is supposed to be Doomsday! But who made this prediction? What evidence did they have? And can anyone truly know when the world will end?
I find this subject particularly interesting because history is full of people who confidently announced dates for the end of the world. Some were religious leaders, others were astrologers, and a few based their conclusions on mathematical calculations. Many attracted devoted followers who believed that the final day had been identified. Yet their predicted dates came and went without the anticipated events. As a Muslim scholar, I see this as an opportunity to remind humanity of a truth established in the Qur’an more than fourteen centuries ago: the world will certainly end, but nobody knows exactly when except Allah.
In 1960, three researchers, Heinz von Foerster, Patricia Mora and Lawrence Amiot, published a paper in the respected scientific journal Science. Its title was rather extraordinary: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. The researchers studied the growth of the world’s population over many centuries. Their mathematical model suggested that if population growth continued indefinitely according to the historical pattern, the population would approach infinity around 2026.
It was an interesting calculation, but it was never a divine prophecy. Nor did it establish that the Earth would be destroyed today. It was a mathematical projection based on assumptions about population growth. Those assumptions have since proved unreliable. Population growth has slowed considerably, and the United Nations now projects that the world’s population will reach approximately 10.3 billion in the 2080s before gradually declining. Nevertheless, the dramatic title of the 1960 paper has continued to attract attention, with some people presenting it as a prediction of the world’s destruction. This reminds me of an important truth: however impressive human calculations may appear, they cannot give us knowledge of everything that lies ahead.
And this is certainly not the first time people have predicted the end of the world. In medieval Europe, certain religious interpretations attached special significance to the years 1000 and 1033. Some believed that history was approaching its final stage, although historians caution that the extent of public panic has often been exaggerated. In 1524, astrologers predicted a catastrophic flood because of a planetary conjunction. The expected worldwide disaster never occurred.
In the nineteenth century, an American preacher named William Miller convinced many followers that the return of Jesus Christ was approaching. Eventually, 22 October 1844 became the expected date. When the day passed without the anticipated event, the disappointment was so great that it became known as the Great Disappointment. In 1988, another prediction announced the approaching Rapture. That date also passed. Harold Camping later predicted major end-time events in 1994 and again in 2011. His predictions did not come true. Then came 21 December 2012, when a misunderstanding of the ancient Maya calendar led many people to believe that the world would end. Again, the anticipated catastrophe did not occur.
And now, in 2026, we are discussing another date. I could mention many more examples, but these are sufficient to show how repeatedly human beings have attempted to determine what lies beyond their knowledge. Some of these predictions were undoubtedly made sincerely. Others involved exaggerated interpretations, sensational publicity or religious manipulation. Whatever the motives, none established the date of the Last Hour.
Now, I want my readers, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, to consider what Islam actually teaches about this matter. Islam does not teach that the world will last forever. On the contrary, the Qur’an repeatedly declares that the Last Hour will certainly come, that the dead will be resurrected, and that every human being will stand before Allah for judgement. However, Allah has deliberately withheld knowledge of the exact time.
In the Qur’an, Allah instructed Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to tell those who asked about the Hour: “Its knowledge rests only with my Lord. None but He will disclose it at its appointed time” (Qur’an 7:187). I invite my readers to reflect carefully upon this verse. The question was asked during the lifetime of the Prophet himself. Yet Allah did not give him a date to announce. Instead, He commanded him to declare that knowledge of the Hour belongs to Allah alone.
In another verse, Allah says: “Indeed, with Allah rests knowledge of the Hour” (Qur’an 31:34). And elsewhere: “People ask you about the Hour. Say: Its knowledge rests only with Allah” (Qur’an 33:63). What could be clearer than these declarations? If Allah instructed His own Messenger to refer knowledge of the Hour to Him, how can any preacher, astrologer, mathematician or self-proclaimed prophet claim to know its exact date?
There is another piece of evidence that I find particularly convincing. In an authentic Hadith recorded by Imam Muslim, Angel Jibrīl appeared before Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asked him several questions concerning Islam and faith. Then Jibrīl asked when the Last Hour would occur. The Prophet replied: “The one being questioned knows no more about it than the one asking” (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Hadith 8).
Consider the significance of this exchange. Jibrīl was the angel entrusted with delivering divine revelation, while Muhammad was Allah’s final Messenger. Yet the Prophet did not announce the date of the Hour. When Jibrīl subsequently asked about its signs, however, the Prophet described some of them. This brings me to an important distinction that I would like everyone to understand: Allah has revealed signs of the approaching Hour, but He has not revealed its precise date.
Among the signs mentioned in authentic Hadiths are the appearance of the Dajjāl, the return of Jesus Christ, the emergence of Gog and Magog, the rising of the Sun from the west and other extraordinary events. But a sign is not a calendar. Knowing that something is approaching does not mean knowing the exact day or hour of its arrival. The Qur’an itself warns that the Hour will come suddenly (Qur’an 7:187; 47:18). Therefore, nobody should turn the signs of the Hour into mathematical calculations and announce a date that Allah has concealed.
Why, then, do people continue predicting the end of the world despite the repeated failures of earlier predictions? I believe several factors are responsible. Human beings naturally fear uncertainty. Whenever wars, earthquakes, epidemics, political crises or unusual events occur, some people become convinced that the end must be immediately upon us. Others are fascinated by numbers and calculations. They combine religious texts, historical dates and astronomical events until they arrive at a particular year or day.
Unfortunately, some religious leaders exploit these fears to attract followers, gain publicity or establish spiritual authority. I consider such behaviour especially dangerous when unsupported predictions are presented as messages from Allah. Religion should guide people towards truth, not frighten them with invented dates. The Qur’an warns us against speaking about Allah without knowledge (Qur’an 7:33). I therefore urge fellow scholars and preachers to distinguish authentic revelation from personal speculation. We should teach people what Allah and His Messenger have actually said, rather than claim knowledge that has not been given to us.
There is another important lesson I want to share. A man once asked Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when the Hour would occur. Instead of announcing a date, the Prophet asked him: “And what have you prepared for it?” (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Hadith 6171; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Hadith 2639). What a remarkable answer! The Prophet directed the man’s attention away from speculation about the future and towards his own responsibility.
That question is just as important today. Whether the world ends during our lifetime or continues for another thousand years, every one of us will eventually die. Allah reminds us: “Every soul shall taste death” (Qur’an 3:185). I do not need to know when the world will end before preparing to meet my Creator. Neither do you. What matters is whether we worship Allah sincerely, fulfil our obligations, treat others justly, avoid wrongdoing and seek His forgiveness. A person who spends his life calculating the Last Hour while neglecting his duties has misunderstood the purpose of the warning.
As I bring this discussion to a close, I want to return to today’s date, Friday, 13 November 2026. Sixty-six years ago, three researchers published a mathematical study that has now become associated with today’s supposed doomsday. The population model on which the claim rested has not been borne out by subsequent demographic developments. But my conviction that nobody knows the date of the Last Hour does not depend upon the success or failure of that calculation. It rests upon the words of Allah.
More than fourteen centuries ago, the Qur’an declared that the Hour would certainly come, but that its appointed time was known only to Allah. The Prophet Muhammad confirmed this principle when questioned by Angel Jibrīl. Although he described signs preceding the Hour, he did not announce its date. No scholar, scientist, preacher, mathematician, astrologer or spiritual leader can legitimately claim certainty concerning a matter that Allah has reserved to Himself.
I am not saying that the world will never end. That would contradict my faith. I am saying that it will end precisely when Allah has decreed, not when a human being predicts. I also do not dismiss the signs of the Hour. I believe in those established by authentic revelation. But I refuse to confuse those signs with knowledge of the precise date.
If someone announces tomorrow that the world will end in 2030, 2050 or 2100, my answer will remain the same. Where is the evidence that Allah has disclosed that date? No amount of mathematical calculation or religious excitement can replace divine knowledge.
As I conclude this article on the very day associated with the 1960 doomsday prediction, I invite every reader to reflect upon the Prophet’s simple but profound question: “What have you prepared for it?” That is the question worth answering.
Let us stop frightening people with unsupported predictions. Let us stop attributing our calculations to Allah. Let us instead prepare for the day when every soul will stand before its Creator.
